name: Question 18
problem:
$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}-4x{y}^{′}=-6{x}^{2}
$$

Consider the differential equation above, for which the corresponding complementary solution is ${y}_{c}(x)=A{x}^{5}+B,$ where $A$ and $B$ are arbitrary constants. Select the correct options below.$\,$
The function ${y}_{p}(x)=x$ 
{{field-1}} 
a particular solution of the differential equation.

$\,$
The function ${y}_{p}(x)={x}^{2}$ 
{{field-2}} 
a particular solution of the differential equation.

$\,$
The general solution of the differential equation is given by

$\,\,$
$y(x)=$ 
{{field-3}}
$+$
{{field-4}},

$\,$
where 
{{field-5}} are arbitrary constants.
worked_solution:
For an inhomogeneous differential equation, the general solution is given by

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

where

- ${y}_{c}(x)$ is the complementary solution (the general solution of the corresponding homogeneous equation), and

- ${y}_{p}(x)$ is a particular solution of the original inhomogeneous equation.

With this in mind, let's check which of the two given functions is a particular solution of our inhomogeneous equation:

- For ${y}_{p}(x)=x,$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(x) & =(x)^{′}=1, \\ {y}^{″}(x) & =(1)^{′}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the equation, we have

$$
{x}^{2}(0)-4x(1)=-6{x}^{2}.\,\,\times 
$$

So, ${y}_{p}(x)=x$ $\text{isn't}$ a particular solution of the differential equation.

- For ${y}_{p}(x)={x}^{2},$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(x) & =({x}^{2})^{′}=2x, \\ {y}^{″}(x) & =(2x)^{′}=2.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the equation, we have

$$
{x}^{2}(2)-4x(2x)=-6{x}^{2}.\,\,✓
$$

So, ${y}_{p}(x)={x}^{2}$ $\text{is}$ a particular solution of the differential equation.

We are told that the complementary solution of our equation is ${y}_{c}(x)=A{x}^{5}+B.$ Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & ={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x) \\  & =A{x}^{5}+B+{x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

where $A\text{ and }B$ are arbitrary constants.

EXPLANATION

For an inhomogeneous differential equation, the general solution is given by y(x)=yc(x)+yp(x), where

  • yc(x) is the complementary solution (the general solution of the corresponding homogeneous equation), and

  • yp(x) is a particular solution of the original inhomogeneous equation.

With this in mind, let's check which of the two given functions is a particular solution of our inhomogeneous equation:

  • For yp(x)=x, we have y′(x)=(x)′=1,y″(x)=(1)′=0. Substituting this into the equation, we have x2(0)−4x(1)=−6x2.× So, yp(x)=x isn't a particular solution of the differential equation.

  • For yp(x)=x2, we have y′(x)=(x2)′=2x,y″(x)=(2x)′=2. Substituting this into the equation, we have x2(2)−4x(2x)=−6x2.✓ So, yp(x)=x2 is a particular solution of the differential equation.

We are told that the complementary solution of our equation is yc(x)=Ax5+B. Therefore, the general solution is y(x)=yc(x)+yp(x)=Ax5+B+x2 where A and B are arbitrary constants.
